newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Vienna sale of looted Jewish art raises $14 mln.
newsitem.headline: Vienna sale of looted Jewish art raises $14 mln.

text.p: An emotionally-charged sale of Austrian Jewish art-works plundered by the Nazis in World War Two raised nearly $15 million for Holocaust victims, four times the original estimate, auctioneers said on Thursday.

The two-day sale of over 8,000 items at the Vienna Museum for Applied Arts, organised by auctioneers Christie's, netted 155 million schillings ($14.5 million) by the time it closed on Wednesday, dwarfing estimates of $3.5 million.

"Our aim, besides raising funds to benefit victims of the Holocaust, was to ensure the sale...took place with the dignity which the original owners of these works of art deserve. I believe this has been achieved," said Paul Grosz, President of Vienna's Jewish community.
Emotions ran high at the packed auction as bidders offered huge prices for the unclaimed works by often little-known artists, whose owners either died in the Holocaust or fled the country.
Paintings and drawings by old masters, miniatures, statues, Flemish tapestries, Albanian arms and a variety of old coins were among the pillaged items that went under the hammer.
Private collectors bought several artworks to donate to museums. Israel's Yad Vashem museum planned to hold an exhibition on Austrian Jewish life before World War Two, Christie's said.
A still life of flowers and insects by 17th century French painter Abraham Mignon, valued at up to 800,000 schillings ($75,000), fetched the top price at 12.7 million schillings.
The highlight of the second day was a rediscovered ancient bust of Alexander the Great from 3 B.C., valued at up to 800,000 schilliings, which went for 2.9 million schillings.

Overall, Christie's said it received over 2,000 commission bids and some 200 more by telephone on 18 lines from all over the world. The scale of international interest was on a par with sales of French Impressionist paintings, it added.
"It has been a very emotional occasion for everyone involved and, we hope, a fitting tribute to the victims of the Holocaust," said Lord Poltimore, director of 19th-century pictures at Christie's.
The auction marked the last chapter in a long-running controversy over Austria's delay in returning the art-works to their owners after receiving them back from the Allies at the end of the war.

Many of the works had been stored for the past 40 years in a monastery in Mauerbach, just outside Vienna. Austria finally returned the works to the Federation of Austrian Jewish Communities last year after a vote in parliament.
Most of the original owners were killed in the Holocaust or fled the country. Just seven items were claimed in the weeks prior to the auction, of which three were returned.
"I would like to think the original owners would be proud to see how their taste has been appreciated in our age," Christie's director Anke Adler-Slottke said after the auction. ($1=10.61 Schilling)
